Thank you for re-submitting your article "Distinct cytoskeletal proteins define zones of enhanced cell wall synthesis in Helicobacter pylori" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, a reviewer previously involved in the original review and a new reviewer. The evaluation has been overseen by Tâm Mignot as a Reviewing Editor and Anna Akhmanova as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

In this re-submission, Taylor and colleagues describe a quantitative characterization of the relationship between two cytoskeletal polymers – MreB and CcmA – and the localization of PG metabolic activity and subsequent cell shape in the helical pathogen Helicobacter pylori. Their major contributions are (1) development of a quantitative framework for describing and analyzing H. pylori cell shape; (2) demonstration of the relationship between local Gaussian curvature of the cell surface and the local incorporation of 2 metabolic probes for PG; (3) the same for the relationship between local Gaussian curvature and localization of cytoskeletal proteins MreB and CcmA; (4) demonstration that MreB is (contrary to a prior report) essential for H. pylori growth; (5) characterization of the in vitro polymerization of CcmA; (6) functional characterization of two point mutants of CcmA that fail to polymerize in vitro; and (7) demonstration of the impact of loss of CcmA function on PG probe incorporation and MreB localization. Collectively these results lead to a model wherein two cytoskeletal systems work to spatially modulate cell wall metabolic activity at regions of different Gaussian curvature to elicit helical cell shape.

Overall the authors went to extreme length to answer the concerns raised by the previous reviewers in a convincing way. There are nevertheless key interpretations issues that would need be addressed before the work can be accepted for publication:

1) The paper now shows convincingly that MreB is essential for growth of H. pylori, which likely is linked to its function in PG synthesis. The model proposes that the recognition of regions of negative curvature by MreB and positive curvature by CcmA underlies the helicity of the H. pylori cell. However, although it is understood that these mechanisms are likely contributing mechanisms, the authors still do not discuss clearly why the action of MreB acting at negative gaussian curvature does not counteract helicity toward Rod restoration. This question is especially important given that a study by Wollrab et al. (bioRxiv 716407; doi:10.1101/716407) questions the MreB negative curvature recognition in E. coli cells. If MreB is indeed localizing to -GC regions in the Helicobacter cell, how do the authors reconcile this with the Wollrab et al. study?

The authors seem to rule out mutual exclusion mechanisms (ie MreB occupies cylindrical parts that CcmA does not occupy) because in subsection “CcmA localization to positive curvature correlates with cell wall synthesis, CcmA polymerization, and

helical cell shape” they conclude that MreB localization is the same in ∆ccmA as in WT. However, there appears to be a difference wherein the relative concentration increases more for MreB at negative curvatures in ∆ccmA than it does in WT and (as the authors actually note later in that section) there is a slight peak of MreB enrichment at ~3 µm-2 in the mutant but not in WT. There also appears to be a dip in concentration around 10-15 µm-2. Importantly, the differences in MreB distribution look to be of a similar magnitude as the differences in D-Ala-alk incorporation between WT and ∆ccmA but the D-Ala-alk incorporation pattern is described as different.

2) For the biochemical characterization of CcmA and mutant forms of CcmA, it would be important to note in the text (not just the Materials and methods) that the proteins are purified in denatured form and refolded to induce/monitor polymer formation. This is important because it does somewhat complicate interpretation of the mutants. It could be that the I55A or L110S mutations influence the ability of CcmA to fold properly during renaturation, rather than having a direct effect on polymerization capacity. The punctate cytoplasmic signal by IF could be consistent with either effect. Related to this, the authors say that the mutants "failed to form any higher order structure under any buffer condition tested". What conditions were tested? Did they test whether the mutants that cannot polymerize were soluble when purified?

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Bonis et al., 2010; Sycuro et al., 2013; Sycuro et al., 2012; Sycuro et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019).

claims.claim: H. pylori CcmA has been shown to self-oligomerize.

claims.claim: CcmA was shown to co-purify with Csd5 and the PG biosynthetic enzyme MurF.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Blair et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In the rod shaped Escherichia coli, MreB helps direct synthesis preferentially to sites at or below zero Gaussian curvature.
claims.source: In the rod shaped Escherichia coli, MreB helps direct synthesis preferentially to sites at or below zero Gaussian curvature. One working model is that this growth pattern promotes rod shape by accelerating growth at dents and restricting growth at bulges along the sidewall, thereby enforcing diameter control (Bratton et al., 2018; Ursell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bratton et al., 2018; Ursell et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In Bacillus subtilis, MreB filaments have been shown to move in paths oriented approximately perpendicular to the long axis of rod shaped cells.
claims.source: In the Gram-positive Bacillus subtilis, MreB filaments have been shown to move in paths oriented approximately perpendicular to the long axis of rod shaped cells. The relative organization of path orientations decreases with an increase in rod diameter, suggesting that filament orientation is sensitive to changes in cell surface curvatures (Hussain et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hussain et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells are 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter.
claims.source: Wild-type cells are 2.5 ± 0.5 µm long and 0.45 ± 0.02 µm in diameter, have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm, and have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells have a helical pitch of 1.7 ± 1 µm.

claims.claim: Wild-type H. pylori cells have a helical diameter of 0.3 ± 0.1 µm.

claims.claim: The average major to minor length ratio in H. pylori is 1.69 ± 0.16.
claims.source: Using the simulated counterparts to these cells, we determined that the average major to minor length ratio is 1.69 ± 0.16, meaning that the major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis in H. pylori.
claims.source: Using the simulated counterparts to these cells, we determined that the average major to minor length ratio is 1.69 ± 0.16, meaning that the major axis is on average 70% longer than the minor axis (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The average Gaussian curvature at the major axis is 5 ± 1 µm−2.
claims.source: We also determined from the simulated cells that the average Gaussian curvature at the major axis is 5 ± 1 µm−2, and the average Gaussian curvature at the minor axis is −11 ± 4 µm−2 (Figure 3H).

claims.claim: The average Gaussian curvature at the minor axis is −11 ± 4 µm−2.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from simulated cells presented in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Supplementation with 4 mg/ml MurNAc partially rescued growth of HJH1 in the presence of 50 µg/ml fosfomycin, but not the parental strain (LSH108).
claims.source: Supplementation with 4 mg/ml MurNAc partially rescued growth of HJH1 in the presence of 50 µg/ml fosfomycin, but not the parental strain (LSH108) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: MurNAc-alk is incorporated into H. pylori peptidoglycan.
claims.source: To verify that clickable MurNAc-alk is indeed incorporated into the cell wall, we purified sacculi from HJH1 labeled with MurNAc-alk for six doublings for MS/MS analysis. We positively identified MurNAc-alk-pentapeptide and MurNAc-alk-tetra-pentapeptide, the most abundant monomeric and dimeric species in the H. pylori cell wall, (Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), as well as less-abundant species (Table 1), confirming incorporation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MS/MS data shown in Figure 4B, C and Table 1.

claims.claim: D-Ala-alk is incorporated exclusively at the pentapeptide position in H. pylori peptidoglycan.
claims.source: To verify that D-Ala-alk is incorporated into the cell wall and to determine the position(s) at which it is incorporated, we purified sacculi from wild-type (LSH100) cells labeled for six doublings for analysis. D-Ala-alk was detected in only pentapeptide monomers and tetra-pentapeptide dimers, indicating that D-Ala-alk is exclusively incorporated at the pentapeptide position (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC and MS data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: MreB is essential in LSH100 H. pylori strain.
claims.source: Since multiple attempts to knock out mreB in wild-type LSH100 were unsuccessful, we generated IM4, a merodiploid strain with a second copy of mreB at a neutral intergenic locus (McGee locus Langford et al., 2006) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) for comparative transformation experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: MreB localization is depleted at the poles in H. pylori.
claims.source: Curvature enrichment analysis of non-dividing cells confirmed that MreB localization is depleted at the poles (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: As Gaussian curvature became more negative, relative MreB concentration increased monotonically.
claims.source: Regardless of whether the poles were included in the analysis, we observed that as Gaussian curvature became more negative, relative MreB concentration increased monotonically (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Wild-type CcmA forms filaments of varying length, long helical bundles of filaments, and lattice structures in vitro.
claims.source: Negative staining of recombinant wild-type CcmA purified from E. coli revealed filaments of varying length, long helical bundles of filaments, and lattice structures (Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8A-B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: CcmA lattices have a filament spacing of 5.5 nm.
claims.source: Fourier transform analysis of the lattice structures revealed a filament spacing of 5.5 nm (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), similar to that previously observed for C. crescentus BacA lattices (5.6 nm) (Vasa et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Fourier transform analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CcmA lattices are skewed with an acute angle of 71.5° and an obtuse angle of 106.2°.
claims.source: While BacA forms orthogonal lattices, the CcmA lattices are skewed (acute angle = 71.5°; obtuse angle = 106.2°).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Fourier transform analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The I55A CcmA variant does not form ordered structures in vitro.
claims.source: While both proteins could be expressed and purified from E. coli (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), the recombinant proteins either fail to form any higher order structures under any buffer condition tested (I55A; Figure 8C) or form no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro (L110S; Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The L110S CcmA variant forms no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro.
claims.source: While both proteins could be expressed and purified from E. coli (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), the recombinant proteins either fail to form any higher order structures under any buffer condition tested (I55A; Figure 8C) or form no lattice structures and many individual filaments in addition to bundles that are straighter, narrower, and shorter than those of wild-type CcmA in vitro (L110S; Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both I55A and L110S CcmA mutant strains displayed a morphology indistinguishable from a ccmA null strain.
claims.source: In both cases, the mutant strains displayed a morphology indistinguishable from a ccmA null strain (Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that formation of higher-order structures by CcmA may be necessary for cell shape-determining functions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell shape analysis data shown in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Wild-type CcmA localizes at the cell boundary as puncta and short arcs and is largely absent from the center of the cell.
claims.source: Wild-type CcmA was observed at the cell boundary as puncta and short arcs and was largely absent from the center of the cell, indicating an association with the cell membrane (Figure 9D and Figure 9—video 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: The mutant CcmA proteins (I55A and L110S) localized as puncta at the center with minimal signal at the cell boundary.
claims.source: In contrast to cells expressing the wild-type version of CcmA, the mutant CcmA proteins localized as puncta at the center with minimal signal at the cell boundary (Figure 9G–J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9G-J.

claims.claim: CcmA has a marked preference for the positive helical axis area.
claims.source: With or without the poles, we saw a marked preference for the positive helical axis area (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1, red line and shaded box) that overlapped with the positive curvature enrichment peaks of MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was no distinguishable curvature preference for I55A or L110S CcmA compared to preimmune serum.
claims.source: There was no distinguishable curvature preference for I55A or L110S CcmA compared to preimmune serum (Figure 10—figure supplement 3A, red and dark red vs. dotted light pink and dotted mauve, respectively), indicating that these proteins are unable to localize preferentially to positive Gaussian surface curvature.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: In ΔccmA cells, MreB curvature preference appears largely similar to wild-type with poles excluded.
claims.source: MreB curvature preference appears largely similar in both wild-type (HJH1, amgK murU, light pink) and ΔccmA with poles excluded (JTH6, amgK murU ΔccmA, dark pink) (Figure 11A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11A.

claims.claim: In ΔccmA cells, MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk patterning change with loss of CcmA; there is greater relative enrichment at low magnitude negative Gaussian curvature compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: In contrast, MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk patterning change with loss of CcmA; there is greater relative enrichment at low magnitude negative Gaussian curvature in ΔccmA cells (dark green and dark blue) compared to wild-type cells (light green and light blue).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11B.

claims.claim: In ΔccmA cells, the enrichment at positive Gaussian curvature is both less pronounced and shifted to lower Gaussian curvature than that of wild-type.
claims.source: Additionally, in ΔccmA cells the enrichment at positive Gaussian curvature is both less pronounced and shifted to lower Gaussian curvature than that of wild-type (Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by curvature enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 11B and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The curved-rod shaped Proteobacteria Caulobacter crescentus and Vibrio cholerae limit relative levels of PG synthesis at negative curvatures through the action of long, cell-spanning cytoskeletal filaments (CreS and CrvA).

claims.claim: Helical cells have a multimodal distribution of sidewall Gaussian curvature that includes an apparent peak at negative curvature and another at positive curvature.

claims.claim: Changing cell length had a negligible impact on the distribution of surface curvatures along the sidewall.

claims.claim: Decreasing the pitch resulted in a helix with tighter coils and a greater distance between the peak of negative and positive Gaussian surface curvatures.

claims.claim: Cells had a greater proportion of sidewall area with positive Gaussian curvature than with negative.

claims.claim: D-Ala-alk showed peaks of enrichment aligning with those of MurNAc-alk, but the magnitude of the peak at positive curvature was reduced.

claims.claim: The mock labeling control showed minimal curvature bias.

claims.source: These data suggest that proper localization of CcmA to the major helical axis may be required for promoting extra cell wall synthesis at the major axis area and patterning helical cell shape.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data from ΔccmA cells shown in Figure 11.

results.result: Wild-type H. pylori cells exhibit helical morphology with distinct geometric parameters (2.5±0.5 µm length, 0.45±0.02 µm diameter, 1.7±1 µm helical pitch, 0.3±0.1 µm helical diameter) that generate a multimodal distribution of sidewall Gaussian curvature with considerably higher positive and negative curvatures than straight- or curved-rod cells. The major axis is 70% longer than the minor axis, with average Gaussian curvatures of 5±1 µm⁻² and −11±4 µm⁻² at the major and minor axes, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C17-C24, and C63-C68 are well-supported by quantitative 3D microscopy data (Figures 2, 3) and computational modeling of cell geometry. The measurements are internally consistent, replicated across multiple cells (n=231 well-fit cells from 1137 total), and the multimodal curvature distribution is clearly demonstrated. The simulation framework validates that helical pitch and diameter are the primary determinants of curvature extremes.

results.result: Quantitative 3D microscopy analysis of 18-minute pulses with MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk metabolic probes demonstrates that cell wall growth is enhanced at both sidewall curvature extremes: enrichment increases monotonically at negative curvatures and peaks near 6 µm⁻² at positive curvatures. Both probes show similar enrichment patterns, though D-Ala-alk shows reduced magnitude at positive curvature. Mock labeling controls show minimal curvature bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C69-C72 are strongly supported by metabolic labeling experiments (Figures 5, 6) with appropriate controls across three biological replicates. The curvature enrichment analysis is quantitative and normalized, with 90% bootstrap confidence intervals. The mock control demonstrates specificity (3.6-4.5% of signal). However, the interpretation that D-Ala-alk reports exclusively on synthesis is complicated by its incorporation mechanism through transpeptidases, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: MreB is essential in H. pylori strain LSH100 and localizes as peripheral foci and short arcs that are depleted at poles and show monotonically increasing enrichment at increasingly negative Gaussian curvatures. Preimmune serum shows no curvature preference despite representing 36.4% of the MreB signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C28-C30, C73-C75 are well-supported by transformation experiments demonstrating essentiality (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence with curvature enrichment analysis (Figure 7, n=1108 cells across three replicates). The essentiality conclusion is strengthened by the merodiploid rescue experiment and the observation that suppressor clones maintained mreB copies. The high preimmune background (36.4%) is concerning but the lack of curvature preference in the control validates the specific enrichment pattern.

results.result: CcmA forms filaments, helical bundles, and skewed lattices (5.5 nm spacing, 71.5°/106.2° angles) in vitro and localizes to the cell boundary as puncta and short arcs in vivo with marked preference for positive Gaussian curvature (peaking near 5 µm⁻²), overlapping with the positive curvature enrichment of MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C31-C33, C37, C39, C76-C77 are supported by TEM data (Figure 8A-B, Figure 8—figure supplement 2) and immunofluorescence with curvature enrichment analysis (Figures 9-10, n=297 cells across three replicates). The in vitro polymerization data clearly demonstrates higher-order structure formation. The in vivo localization shows specific enrichment at positive curvature with appropriate controls (no-FLAG control at 28.9% of signal). The correlation between CcmA localization and synthesis probe enrichment is compelling.

results.result: CcmA point mutants I55A and L110S show altered polymerization properties in vitro (I55A forms no structures; L110S forms shorter, straighter bundles without lattices) and fail to localize to positive curvature in vivo, resulting in rod-shaped cells indistinguishable from ccmA null strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C34-C36, C38, C40 are well-supported by TEM data (Figure 8C-D), cell shape analysis (Figure 8F, n>300 cells per strain), and immunofluorescence with curvature enrichment analysis (Figures 9-10, Figure 10—figure supplement 3). The mutants show consistent loss of both in vitro polymerization and in vivo function. However, the I55A mutant shows lower steady-state protein levels, which could contribute to the phenotype independently of polymerization defects.

results.result: The authors propose a model where CcmA and MreB promote peptidoglycan synthesis at positive and negative Gaussian curvatures, respectively, and that this patterning is one mechanism necessary for maintaining helical shape. Proper localization of CcmA to the major helical axis may be required for promoting extra cell wall synthesis at the major axis area.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C81 represent the central mechanistic model, which is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) MreB and CcmA show complementary curvature preferences, (2) synthesis probes show enrichment matching protein localizations, (3) CcmA mutants lose both localization and helical shape, and (4) ΔccmA cells show altered synthesis patterns. However, the model is explicitly presented as a proposal and the authors acknowledge that additional mechanisms are likely required, as the synthesis pattern alone seems insufficient to fully explain helical shape maintenance.

results.result: In ΔccmA cells, MreB curvature preference remains similar to wild-type (with poles excluded), but MurNAc-alk and D-Ala-alk patterning changes: there is greater relative enrichment at low magnitude negative Gaussian curvature and the enrichment at positive Gaussian curvature is less pronounced and shifted to lower curvature compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by curvature enrichment analysis of ΔccmA cells (Figure 11, n=814 MreB, n=686 MurNAc-alk, n=1386 D-Ala-alk cells across three replicates). The data demonstrate that loss of CcmA alters synthesis patterning while MreB localization is largely maintained. This supports the model that CcmA specifically promotes synthesis at positive curvature. However, the interpretation is complicated by the fact that ΔccmA cells have different geometry (rod-shaped), which affects the normalization and interpretation of curvature enrichment.

results.result: The engineered H. pylori strain HJH1 (expressing AmgK and MurU) can utilize exogenous MurNAc, as demonstrated by partial rescue from fosfomycin treatment (MIC=25 µg/ml) with 4 mg/ml MurNAc supplementation. MS/MS analysis confirms incorporation of MurNAc-alk into peptidoglycan pentapeptides and tetra-pentapeptides, while D-Ala-alk is incorporated exclusively at the pentapeptide position.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27, C60 are well-supported by fosfomycin rescue experiments (Figure 4A), MIC determination (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and MS/MS analysis (Figure 4B-D, Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplements 3-4). The biochemical validation is thorough and demonstrates that both probes are incorporated into the cell wall. The exclusive pentapeptide incorporation of D-Ala-alk is clearly demonstrated by HPLC and MS data.

results.result: Background and contextual claims about H. pylori biology, bacterial cell shape mechanisms, and prior work on MreB, bactofilins, and cell wall synthesis in various organisms. These include established facts about H. pylori (helical bacterium causing gastric disease, genetically tractable), peptidoglycan structure determining cell shape, requirements for helical shape maintenance proteins, MreB function in other bacteria, and bactofilin functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C16, C44-C62 are background/contextual claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature or represent established knowledge in the field. These provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings but are not primary results of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.
